client: I got rejected from my dream university last week, and I can't stop feeling like a complete failure. Everyone around me seems to be moving forward while I'm stuck here questioning if I'm even good enough. Part of me wonders if talking about it will help - it's not like words can change the fact that I didn't make the cut.
therapist: I hear how painful this rejection feels for you, and how it's shaking your confidence. While you're questioning if talking will help, I notice your voice sounds more subdued than your words suggest - would you say there's also some exhaustion or numbness mixed in with these feelings?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I guess I am exhausted. It's like I put everything into this one goal for years, and now I just feel empty. People keep telling me to "look at other options," but that just makes me feel more numb - like they don't understand how much this meant to me.
therapist: It sounds like this loss has left you feeling disconnected, both from your dreams and from the people trying to support you. When you mention feeling empty, I wonder if that numbness might be protecting you from the full weight of this disappointment right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Maybe it is protection... but I don't know if that's helpful. The emptiness just makes me feel more alone. And honestly, I'm kind of angry at myself for caring this much - like maybe if I hadn't pinned all my hopes on this one school, I wouldn't be such a wreck now.
therapist: Your voice sounds more intense than before as you describe this—like there's real energy in your frustration with yourself. That anger seems to be fighting with the emptiness you mentioned earlier—would you say it feels like different parts of you are pulling in opposite directions right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, that's exactly how it feels - like part of me wants to scream and break something, but another part just wants to curl up and disappear. I don't know which feeling is worse. And I'm mad at myself for not being able to just "get over it" like everyone expects me to. 

Sometimes I think the anger is easier to handle than the emptiness because at least it makes me feel something. But then I worry the anger is making me push people away when they're trying to help.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between these two powerful emotions—the anger that gives you energy and the emptiness that feels overwhelming. I'm noticing how your voice lifts when you talk about the anger—does that part of you feel more familiar or safe in some way compared to the emptiness?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, anger does feel safer because at least it's something I can direct - either at myself or at the unfairness of it all. The emptiness just makes me feel small and powerless, like I don't even matter. But I know neither feeling is healthy, and that just makes me more frustrated with myself for not handling this better.
therapist: It makes sense that you'd gravitate toward the anger when the alternative feels so disorienting—like choosing between two difficult options. I notice your voice has more energy when you talk about this frustration with yourself—almost like there's a part of you that's still fighting to regain control amidst all this pain.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That fight for control is exhausting though. Part of me wonders if I should just stop fighting altogether—maybe if I accept that I'm not good enough, the pain will go away faster. But then another part of me is terrified of giving up completely, because what if that means I'll never try for anything big again?
therapist: Your words and voice carry such tension—like you're caught between the fear of giving up completely and the terror of continuing to fight. That fast, high-pitched urgency makes me wonder—is part of this struggle about not wanting to lose the version of yourself that dared to dream big in the first place?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That... that actually makes me want to cry. Because yeah, that ambitious version of me feels like she's slipping away, and I don't know how to hold onto her without the dream that defined her. But I'm also scared that if I let her go completely, there'll be nothing left of me worth fighting for.
therapist: It sounds like you're grieving not just the lost opportunity, but also the version of yourself that felt defined by that dream—and that grief comes through so clearly in your voice right now. The fear that there might be "nothing left worth fighting for" without that identity—that's a profound fear to sit with, isn't it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I never thought about it like that before. It's like I'm mourning who I was supposed to become, and now I'm terrified of who I'll be instead. But isn't this kind of thinking just making things worse? Shouldn't I be trying to move forward instead of getting stuck in this grief?
therapist: What I hear is this important tension—between the pressure to "move forward" and the very real need to honor this grief about who you thought you'd become. Your voice has such urgency when you ask if you're making things worse—might that pressure to move on actually be cutting you off from something important you need to process first?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I never considered that rushing to move on might be part of the problem. But sitting with this grief feels dangerous somehow—like if I stop to really feel it, I might completely fall apart. At the same time, I'm exhausted from pretending I'm okay when I'm not.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two fears—the fear of falling apart if you fully feel this grief, and the exhaustion of keeping it all together. Your voice carries a lot of intensity right now—like you're holding something heavy that deserves to be set down, even if just for a moment. Would you say there's any small way you could let yourself rest from this pressure to either "fall apart" or "pretend to be okay"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: Maybe I could try letting myself just feel whatever comes up for an hour each day without judging it. But I'm scared that once I start, I won't be able to stop the flood of emotions. What if that hour turns into days of just crying and not functioning?
therapist: It's understandable to feel scared about opening up to these emotions—your voice sounds softer and more tentative as you share this fear. What if we worked on setting up some gentle boundaries around that hour, so you can dip your toes into these feelings without feeling overwhelmed by them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
